newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - bonus for refiners.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - bonus for refiners.

text.p: Gulf oil refiners can look forward to more rich pickings in the coming week though traders caution that the market is set to correct itself before resuming its upward winter-led momentum, regional traders said on Thursday.
Gulf product prices have leapt this month to fresh five-year highs on surging European and U.S. heating fuel markets despite ebbing Far East import demand.
Gas oil (diesel) was assessed at a five-year high of $28.85 a barrel fob Gulf on Thursday, compared to year-on-year $18.45.
Sellers of 0.5 percent sulphur material aimed for a $1 premium to independent price quotes.
Gas oil prices have rallied 32 percent since mid June, outpacing a 18 percent gain in regional benchmark Dubai crude and providing the backbone to firm Gulf refining margins.
This has led some term customers to ask for full contractural product volumes in the coming months, regular term lifters contacted in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait said.
Though traders expect prices will take ease before stepping higher, the rally may remain intact ahead of the northern hemisphere winter and delays in the resumption of Iraq exports.
For the region's oil heavyweights the product price rally is an added bonus to crude strength.
That is in addition to lavishing Gulf producers billions of dollars in windfall revenue.
Posted prices from refiners in Kuwait, Bahrain and Saudi Arabia have all followed the market higher this week.
Short-term, Gulf product markets will take their lead from European and Indian distillate demand, traders said.
Fundamentally the Gulf remains tigh with available spot cargoes placed into the Mediterranean, east Africa and the Indian subcontinent.
Egypt's tender to buy up to 150,000 tonnes of 0.5 percent sulphur was also seen as generally supportive.
"The position is the same. Gas oil cannot be found, jet is difficult but is being placed...Naphtha can bank on Asia," one Gulf-based trader said.
Traders said the market would take its next decisive turn when India Oil Corp (IOC) awards its tender for the supply of high speed diesel in December in the final week of October.

IOC fourth-quarter purchasing has so far disappointed, culminating in the cancellation of November needs. But traders were optimistic that IOC would award at least three cargoes in its December tender, though Asian traders feared Indian port congestion and additional term supplies may limit purchases.
An IOC official on Thursday confirmed that the company was in talks with Saudi Aramco for middle distillate supplies but said that discussion was "still very fluid."
Jet-kerosene markets were subdued with cargoes available for Far East and Mediterranean destinations.
"The price is not attractive for the eastern market," one trader in the region said.
Asian petrochemical demand was seen robust enough to sustain Gulf naphtha prices at current post Gulf War highs of $200.20 a tonne.
-- Steven Swindells, Dubai Newsroom, +971 4 6071255
